summary.title: Embracing Generative AI in Construction through a Quantitative Analysis and Weighted Score Ranking of Perceptions, Applications, and Complexities
summary.topic: BIM compliance checking; Cost estimation; Scheduling; Safety monitoring; Design review; Quality control
summary.abstract: As generative artificial intelligence (AI) tools such as generative pretrained transformer-based language models gain prominence, the construction industry faces adoption challenges that differ from deterministic tools. Generative AI (GenAI) is probabilistic, multifunctional, and cognitively demanding, requiring prompting skills, interpretability, and data governance-factors not fully captured by traditional technology acceptance model (TAM) and unified theory of acceptance and use of technology (UTAUT) applications. Addressing this gap, this study assesses how US construction professionals perceive both the benefits and complexities of GenAI, identifies which applications they prioritize, and segments adoption profiles across the workforce. A nationwide survey of 97 companies revealed three benefit dimensions-Real-Time Construction Intelligence, Regulatory and Analytical Automation, and Design Acceleration and Enhancement-and three complexity dimensions-Organizational and Change Management, Data and Customization, and Integration and Cultural Alignment-through exploratory factor analysis. Weighted ranking placed Design Time Reduction, Building Information Model (BIM) Enhancement,…
summary.results: Construction professionals perceive GenAI benefits (Real-Time Construction Intelligence, Regulatory/Analytical Automation, Design Acceleration) as significantly outweighing complexities (Organizational/Change Management, Data/Customization, Integration/Cultural Alignment), with a large effect size (d=1.318). Design Time Reduction, BIM Enhancement, and Risk Assessment Support were top-ranked benefits, while Risk Assessment Challenges, Data Availability, and Real-Time Deployment were top barriers. Cluster analysis revealed four distinct adoption profiles where training moderated polarization and highly familiar users were often the most critical.
summary.gaps: No prior empirical study has systematically applied TAM/UTAUT to GenAI in construction, segmented practitioners by familiarity/training, or quantitatively captured both benefits and complexities of GenAI adoption in the sector.
summary.future: Future work should include longitudinal tracking of GenAI perception changes, experimental evaluations of training interventions, cross-country and cross-stakeholder comparative studies, and qualitative methods to unpack nuanced reasoning. Additional constructs such as trust in AI and perceived ethical risk should be incorporated, and academic perspectives should complement industry viewpoints.

summary.title: Navigating New Frontiers in Construction Disputes: Strategically Adopting Smart Contracts and Technology Assisted Review
summary.topic: Contract management; Other
summary.abstract: Recent technological advancements offer new possibilities for managing and resolving disputes in the construction sector, particularly through the application of Smart Contracts and Technology Assisted Review. Smart Contracts, leveraging blockchain technology, automate the enforcement of contractual obligations, while Technology Assisted Review employs Artificial Intelligence to facilitate efficient legal document review. The primary objective of this article is to identify and analyze legal issues associated with the implementation of these technologies in construction projects, emphasizing the necessity of a cautious, legally informed approach to their adoption. The methodological framework comprises an analysis of relevant literature, legal cases, and legislative contexts across multiple jurisdictions, highlighting both practical advantages and associated challenges. Within the scope of this article, these technologies are examined through a theoretical framework grounded in the rule of law. Despite their increasing recognition and benefits, this article identifies insufficiencies within existing legal frameworks governing their implementation. The article underscores the…
summary.results: Smart contracts can automate contractual performance and reduce ambiguity-driven disputes, while TAR can dramatically reduce document review burdens in large construction litigation, as evidenced by cases like McConnell Dowell v. Santam. However, smart contracts' rigidity threatens fairness in unforeseen circumstances (e.g., frustration doctrine), and TAR's 'black box' algorithms challenge transparency and judicial accountability. Adoption must be balanced against core judicial values under the rule of law.
summary.gaps: Existing legal frameworks insufficiently govern smart contracts and TAR in construction, and there is limited direct scholarship linking TAR's capabilities to the broader construction field beyond narrow discovery applications.
summary.future: The paper calls for development of legal frameworks that accommodate smart contracts and TAR while preserving judicial values, and encourages stakeholders to engage in shaping regulation. It notes the difficulty of drawing firm conclusions at this evolving stage and implicitly invites further jurisdictional and doctrinal analysis.

summary.title: Improving Access to Building Licensing Information in Australia: Design and Development of a Graph-Based Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) Artificial Intelligence (AI) System
summary.topic: Permitting; Other
summary.abstract: Digital technologies have been widely adopted to improve efficiency, transparency, and decision making in the construction industry. However, regulatory processes such as building license and registration applications remain complex, fragmented, and difficult for applicants to navigate, particularly for early career practitioners and small businesses. This study presents the design and development of a graph-based retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) artificial intelligence (AI) system that assists users in applying for building licenses and registrations in Australia. By integrating eight regulatory burden frameworks, this study identified ten categories of licensing-related burden. A three-layer system architecture was subsequently proposed for the Australian construction licensing context, and a prototype is implemented using the New South Wales (NSW) regulatory framework. The system provides context-aware responses, step-by-step guidance, and tailored information based on user queries, thereby reducing regulatory burden for individuals, companies, and industry bodies. Prototype evaluation against general-purpose AI tools indicates improved information accessibility and reduced…
summary.results: The graph-based RAG prototype outperformed ChatGPT (GPT-4o) and Google Search AI Overview (Gemini 2.5) across most evaluation metrics, achieving higher accuracy (0.78), evidence support (0.83), and actionability (0.81), and was ranked as the best response in 72% of cases. Grounding the system in official government documentation and using graph-structured reasoning improved information accuracy, traceability, and contextual relevance for licensing queries. The prototype demonstrated potential to reduce information, administrative, substantive compliance, and non-compliance-related regulatory burdens.
summary.gaps: Few, if any, studies apply graph-based RAG to support building, trade, and specialist licensing processes in the Australian construction industry, and existing AI approaches rely on general-purpose LLMs that raise concerns about information accuracy, traceability, and consistency in regulatory contexts.
summary.future: Future work includes automating regulatory updates via scheduled crawling, expanding coverage from NSW to all Australian states and territories, and adding multilingual and accessibility support. The reasoning layer will be enhanced with improved prompt strategies, confidence-aware reasoning, and better evidence transparency, while the interface will add audio input, file upload, and visual process diagrams. Large-scale user testing and extension to other engineering regulatory domains (e.g.,…

summary.title: Applying Action Research to Developing a GPT-Based Assistant for Construction Cost Code Verification in State-Funded Projects in Vietnam
summary.topic: Cost estimation; BIM compliance checking
summary.ai_model: NLP/LLM; Generative AI; Rule-based system; Hybrid
summary.abstract: Cost code verification in state-funded construction projects remains a labor-intensive and error-prone task, particularly given the structural heterogeneity of project estimates and the prevalence of malformed codes, inconsistent units of measurement (UoMs), and locally modified price components. This study evaluates a deterministic GPT-based assistant designed to automate Vietnam’s regulatory verification. The assistant was developed and iteratively refined across four Action Research cycles. Also, the system enforces strict rule sequencing and dataset grounding via Python-governed computations. Rather than relying on probabilistic or semantic reasoning, the system performs strictly deterministic checks on code validity, UoM alignment, and unit price conformity in material (MTR), labor (LBR), and machinery (MCR), given the provincial unit price books (UPBs). Deterministic equality is evaluated either on raw numerical values or on values transformed through explicitly declared, rule-governed operations, preserving auditability without introducing tolerance-based or inferential reasoning. A dedicated exact-match mechanism, which is activated only when a code is invalid, enables the…
summary.results: The deterministic GPT-based assistant reliably executed verification steps across heterogeneous spreadsheet formats, correctly identifying typographical code errors only when full price vectors exactly matched normative entries while conservatively classifying other cases as unlisted (TT) items. Practitioner feedback confirmed that the line-by-line auditable outputs reduced manual tracing effort and improved evaluation consistency. The study demonstrates that tightly constrained LLMs can function as dependable rule-execution engines rather than probabilistic reasoners in compliance-critical tasks.
summary.gaps: No existing research integrates LLM-driven reasoning with numerical verification for cost code checking, and prior AI studies in AEC do not address mis-typed code recovery, partial price-component edits, or deterministic LLM-based verification aligned with regulatory requirements.
summary.future: Extending the framework to support multi-sheet and hierarchical cost structures, integrating BIM-derived quantity and cost data, supporting multi-provincial and cross-jurisdictional UPB datasets, and testing the system in live verification environments with real-time document flows and collaborative workflows.

summary.title: Framework for automated building code compliance checking to improve transparency, trust, validation, and design interpretation
summary.topic: BIM compliance checking; Design review; Permitting
summary.ai_model: NLP/LLM; Ontology/Knowledge graph; Rule-based system; Hybrid
summary.abstract: Building codes are complex and written in natural language, making interpretation costly and prone to error. This paper addresses the specific question of how Natural Language Processing (NLP) can automate code compliance checking across entire building codes rather than isolated sections. The proposed framework uses a two-stage method that first structures code documents into semantic hierarchies and then applies ontological reasoning to generate and verify rule sets against BIM models. Results show that the approach captures exceptions and cross-references more effectively than current rule-based or commercial systems. This is important for architects and engineers who must ensure accuracy, transparency, and trust in compliance decisions while reducing manual effort. The framework also establishes a foundation for scalable, fully automated compliance systems that can guide future research on integrating artificial intelligence with building regulations. © 2025 Elsevier B.V. All rights are reserved, including those for text and data mining, AI training, and similar technologies.
summary.results: The proposed framework successfully extracted rules, exceptions, and cross-references across multiple building codes (IBC, IFC, IRC) and outperformed both ChatGPT-based code generation and commercial Solibri software in completeness, accuracy, and handling of exceptions/inferred sections. Usability evaluation with five practitioners showed high trust (4.27/5) and clarity ratings (4.53/5) for the system outputs. The approach maintains determinism and transparency, enabling designers to inspect and refine generated rules unlike black-box LLM or commercial solutions.
summary.gaps: No systematic framework exists that comprehensively handles nested building code structures, exceptions, and cross-references while maintaining transparency; LLM-based approaches suffer from non-determinism, while commercial rule-based tools are opaque and not scalable across code versions.
summary.future: Future work should incorporate data from tables, figures, and images during extraction, handle curved/spherical geometries, and address fragmented text in PDFs. The framework should be extended to external building components, site-level conditions (setbacks, property boundaries), and additional regulatory domains for multi-disciplinary compliance checks.

summary.title: Open the ‘Black Box’ of Large Language Models and Make Them Explainable in Construction
summary.topic: Safety monitoring; Scheduling; Quality control; BIM compliance checking; Design review; Other
summary.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly being applied to support decision-making in construction. Yet, their value is constrained by opaque internal reasoning processes that limit trust, verification, and accountable use. Although several studies demonstrate the potential of LLMs for tasks such as safety monitoring, scheduling, quality management, and information retrieval enabled by building information modeling, explainable AI (XAI) has not been systematically incorporated into their design or deployment. Such an omission heightens the risks of hallucinations, bias, and unverifiable outputs in safety-critical, cost-sensitive, and highly regulated project settings. This paper examines how local and global XAI techniques can be adapted to make LLM-based systems transparent and operationally valuable in construction. It synthesises emerging specific applications and provides a mapping of explanation methods to everyday decision tasks in construction, highlighting how XAI can contribute to more interpretable, defensible, and trustworthy outputs from LLMs. To support continued progress in the emerging area of inquiry, this paper outlines key research questions focused on…
summary.results: Traditional XAI techniques such as LIME and SHAP are insufficient for LLMs due to their scale, contextual token interactions, and emergent reasoning; therefore, LLM-specific methods (gradient-based, attention, counterfactual, chain-of-thought, RAG, probing, mechanistic interpretability) must be adapted and embedded throughout LLM design and deployment in construction. The authors argue that without explainability, LLM outputs in safety-critical, cost-sensitive, and regulated construction contexts remain unverifiable and untrustworthy, and they illustrate how specific XAI methods map to tasks like hazard detection, scheduling, NCR classification, BIM retrieval, and risk management.
summary.gaps: XAI has not been systematically incorporated into LLM design or deployment in construction, and the CEM literature overlooks the need to make LLM behavior interpretable for diverse stakeholders; adoption remains fragmented, focused on single use cases, and lacks sector-specific evaluation criteria, unified design guidance, and transparency around LLM reasoning.
summary.future: Future research should address transparent architectural design of LLMs, techniques to trace intermediate reasoning in construction tasks, context-aware explanations tailored to different stakeholders, bias detection and mitigation in construction datasets (NCRs, incident reports, BIM, progress logs), and metrics/protocols to evaluate explanation clarity, fidelity, trustworthiness, and utility. The authors also call for openness in sharing models, code, and datasets to support reproducibility…

summary.title: Responsible AI in Construction Safety: Systematic Evaluation of Large Language Models and Prompt Engineering
summary.topic: Safety monitoring; Worker monitoring; Other
summary.abstract: Responsible artificial intelligence (AI) in construction safety requires rigorous, domain-specific evaluation. Deploying large language models (LLMs) without understanding their capabilities and limitations risks generating inaccurate information and compromising worker safety. This study benchmarked three leading LLMs - GPT-3.5, GPT-4o, and Gemini 2.0 Flash - using 385 Board of Certified Safety Professionals exam questions across seven knowledge areas. All models achieved passing scores (GPT-4o: 84.6%, Gemini: 80.8%, GPT-3.5: 73.8%), demonstrating strengths in the knowledge areas of safety management systems and hazard identification. However, LLMs performed relatively poorly in science and math, emergency response, and fire prevention. Error analysis identified four key limitations impacting performance: knowledge gaps, reasoning flaws, memory issues, and calculation errors. This study also highlights the impact of four prompt engineering factors, with variations in accuracy reaching 13.5% for GPT-3.5, 7.9% for GPT-4o, and 10.4% for Gemini. However, no single prompt configuration has proven universally effective across three models and seven knowledge areas, suggesting the need…
summary.results: GPT-4o (84.6%), Gemini 2.0 Flash (80.8%), and GPT-3.5 (73.8%) all passed BCSP exams, performing best in safety management and hazard identification but weakly in science/math, emergency response, and fire prevention. Four recurring error types were identified: knowledge gaps, reasoning flaws, memory issues, and calculation errors. Prompt engineering factors influenced accuracy by up to 13.5%, but no single prompt configuration was universally optimal across models or knowledge areas, indicating the need for model- and task-specific optimization.
summary.gaps: There is a lack of domain-specific evaluation of LLMs in construction safety, and prompt engineering effects and structured output requirements in safety contexts remain underexplored. Consistency and reliability of LLM responses in safety applications have also not been systematically assessed.
summary.future: Future work should explore retrieval-augmented generation, fine-tuning, agentic workflows, and integration of external math tools to address knowledge gaps, reasoning flaws, and calculation errors. Researchers should also benchmark broader LLMs (Claude, LLaMA, Grok), test open-ended and multilingual safety tasks, and evaluate LLMs in multi-turn conversational settings that reflect real practitioner use.

summary.title: Automated “E”-aware data processing for construction ESG using building information modeling and large language model
summary.topic: Other
summary.ai_model: NLP/LLM; Generative AI; Computer vision; Other
summary.abstract: Environmental, Social and Governance (ESG) assessment and disclosure are critical for architecture, engineering, and construction (AEC) companies to market their financial results, reputational position, and compliance with regulatory requirements. Within this framework, the environmental (“E”) dimension presents unique and formidable data management challenges distinct from social and governance aspects. Specifically, the complex interplay of quantitative metrics and qualitative descriptions within ‘E’-aware data (e.g., measurable resource consumption alongside descriptive material sourcing practices, emissions figures coupled with compliance narratives), amplified by its sheer volume and the persistent ambiguity of environmental indicators and reporting standards, poses significant obstacles to effective ‘E’-aware data disclosure. Large Language Models (LLMs) possess inherent advantages in processing such complex environmental information due to their proficient language processing and generalization capabilities. Nonetheless, the development of LLM-based methods explicitly tailored for environmental data management within the construction sector remains underexplored. To this…
summary.results: The proposed framework successfully automates E-aware data extraction with 84.43% accuracy and saves 64.4% of processing time compared to manual methods. BIM-based carbon emission calculations achieved near-perfect consistency with manual calculations (error <0.03%), and the locally-deployed Llama 3 with RAG improved accuracy by 13.8% over general LLM approaches while preserving data confidentiality. Fifteen construction-specific E-aware indicators were derived from mainstream ESG frameworks.
summary.gaps: The paper identifies two main gaps: lack of domain knowledge on E-aware data sources in AEC construction projects, and lack of automated LLM-based E-data extraction approaches tailored to construction ESG requirements with complex structured data.
summary.future: Future work should improve dynamic adaptability of the E-aware knowledge graph to accommodate evolving indicators and construction updates, and implement targeted fine-tuning of LLMs for construction-specific nuances and terminologies. Multimodal data integration (site imagery, sensor feeds) and expansion of material libraries for non-standard/innovative construction materials are also needed.

summary.title: Generative AI for Sustainable Development in the Construction Industry: Exploring Organizational Adoption Patterns
summary.topic: Design review; Scheduling; Safety monitoring; Cost estimation; Other
summary.abstract: While Generative AI (GenAI) is a critical enabler for achieving key United Nations Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) in the construction industry, organizations remain hesitant to implement it due to limited awareness of key barriers and the absence of clear adoption strategies. This study aims to (1) identify key barriers and propose strategies for GenAI adoption in the construction industry, and (2) examine how the significance of barriers and the effectiveness of strategies vary across organizations of different types and sizes. Through a systematic literature review and pilot interviews, this study identified 23 barriers and 17 strategies, which were then evaluated using statistical analysis and post-survey interviews. The findings reveal that “Unclear Legal Liability,” “Lack of Explainability,” and “Lack of Accuracy/Precision” are the most significant barriers, while there is an industry-wide preference for a passive “wait-and-see” stance, prioritizing external, government-led initiatives over driving internal change for GenAI adoption. The study further uncovers notable differences in barrier significance and strategy effectiveness across organizational contexts. This…
summary.results: The most significant barriers to GenAI adoption are unclear legal liability, lack of explainability, and lack of accuracy/precision, while organizations show a preference for passive, externally-driven strategies like government-industry collaboration rather than internal transformation. Contractors perceive legal liability as more significant than developers, creating a 'liability gap', and large enterprises prioritize fault tolerance and output validation while SMEs depend on external incentives and regulatory clarity. Consultants' barrier rankings correlate strongly with contractors' and moderately with developers', positioning them as knowledge mediators across the value chain.
summary.gaps: Existing literature lacks prioritization of barriers' relative significance across organizational types and sizes, and proposed strategies are fragmented without evaluation of effectiveness across varying organizational conditions.
summary.future: Future studies should revisit findings as GenAI matures and longitudinal evidence emerges from real-world projects. Research should also explore GenAI adoption at the individual practitioner level (architects, project managers, quantity surveyors) to support role-specific workforce development and targeted strategies.

summary.title: Artificial Intelligence Ethics in Municipal and Construction Sectors: A Literature Review
summary.topic: Permitting; Safety monitoring; Quality control; Design review; Facility management
summary.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) technologies are increasingly used to improve the efficiency of public services such as building permit approvals, zoning management, and infrastructure inspections. However, this rapid integration has raised ethical concerns related to algorithmic bias, transparency, accountability, and data privacy. For example, automated zoning systems may inadvertently prioritize certain areas owing to biased data inputs. This paper presents a systematic literature review and bibliometric analysis focused on ethical AI frameworks in municipal and construction-related services, particularly focusing on the United Arab Emirates (UAE), where smart city initiatives are rapidly advancing. The review followed preferred reporting items for systematic reviews and meta-analyses (PRISMA) guidelines and drew on 102 peer-reviewed articles from Scopus, IEEE Xplore, and EBSCOhost using keywords such as “AI ethics”, “smart cities”, and “public services”. The analysis highlights recurring ethical gaps in existing global frameworks, including limited adaptability to local cultural and regulatory environments. Drawing from best practices in the European Union Artificial Intelligence…
summary.results: Bias (80%), transparency (72%), accountability (60%), and privacy (52%) are the dominant ethical concerns in AI municipal/construction research, and the EU AI Act is the most cited governance framework. Existing global frameworks lack adaptability to the UAE's cultural, legal, and regulatory context, requiring localized adaptations. The proposed framework operationalizes high-level principles into workflow-level, audit-ready controls (risk tiering, layered transparency, empowered oversight) for permits, inspections, and infrastructure monitoring.
summary.gaps: Global AI governance frameworks lack cultural and regional adaptability, particularly for UAE municipal and construction contexts, and empirical validation of ethical frameworks in real-world public-sector AI deployments is largely missing.
summary.future: Develop UAE-specific ethical AI frameworks incorporating human oversight, bias mitigation, and legal accountability. Conduct empirical case studies in UAE municipalities to validate proposed frameworks and calibrate harm thresholds. Explore dynamic regulatory frameworks that evolve alongside emerging AI technologies.

summary.title: Toward Responsible AI in High-Stakes Domains: A Dataset for Building Static Analysis with LLMs in Structural Engineering
summary.topic: Structural design; Design review
summary.abstract: Modern engineering increasingly operates within socio-technical networks, such as the interdependence of energy grids, transport systems, and building codes, where decisions must be reliable and transparent. Large language models (LLMs) such as GPT promise efficiency by interpreting domain-specific queries and generating outputs, yet their predictive nature can introduce biases or fabricated values—risks that are unacceptable in structural engineering, where safety and compliance are paramount. This work presents a dataset that embeds generative AI into validated computational workflows through the Model Context Protocol (MCP). MCP enables API-based integration between ChatGPT (GPT-4o) and numerical solvers by converting natural-language prompts into structured solver commands. This creates context-aware exchanges—for example, transforming a query on seismic drift limits into an OpenSees analysis—whose results are benchmarked against manually generated ETABS models. This architecture ensures traceability, reproducibility, and alignment with seismic design standards. The dataset contains prompts, GPT outputs, solver-based analyses, and comparative error metrics for four reinforced…
summary.results: The GPT+MCP framework produces structural analysis results nearly identical to benchmark ETABS outputs (relative errors <1.5%), while direct GPT-only prompting yielded errors of 230-270%, demonstrating the hallucination risk of unconstrained LLMs. The MCP-integrated workflow reduced runtime from 12-15 minutes (manual ETABS) to 6-12 seconds, showing feasibility for practical design verification while preserving computational fidelity and compliance with seismic codes.
summary.gaps: LLMs generate statistical predictions rather than verifiable computations, producing hallucinations that are a critical barrier to safe adoption in high-stakes structural engineering where context-aware frameworks anchored in validated workflows are lacking.
summary.future: Extension of the MCP framework to other domains such as energy modelling, HVAC analysis, sustainability-driven optimisation, and BIM-linked generative workflows. The dataset is also proposed as a template for introducing greater complexity including different materials, nonlinear analysis procedures, and structural optimisation, as well as for educational applications.

summary.title: Long context window-based zero-shot legal interpretation of building codes and regulations
summary.topic: Permitting; BIM compliance checking; Design review
summary.abstract: South Korean authorities handle over 2000 inquiries daily about building code violations. Interpreting these complex, frequently updated codes is challenging, even for legal experts. Prior studies using large language models (LLMs) with retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) have struggled with context loss due to data segmentation. This paper proposes three automated building code interpreter (ABCI) models—Original, Inferred, and Filtered—that leverage long-context window (LCW) LLMs as the base model. On 171 challenging legal interpretative question-answering (LIQA) cases, ABCI-Filtered achieved 63.2 % accuracy, outperforming the RAG baseline approach (56.1 %), state-of-the-art LLMs like Claude 3.7 (60.2 %), as well as ABCI-Inferred (60.8 %) and ABCI-Original (56.7 %). Notably, unlike prior methods that require fine-tuning, ABCI-Filtered outperformed previous methods using only zero-shot reasoning. In an additional experiment using a relatively straightforward building code QA dataset, ABCI-Filtered and ABCI-Inferred outperformed the other methods (79.6 % and 80.0 %, respectively), confirming the difficulty of the initial task using the LIQA dataset. © 2025
summary.results: ABCI-Filtered achieved 63.2% accuracy on the challenging LIQA dataset, outperforming the RAG-based SPARC Precision baseline (56.1%) and SOTA LLMs like Claude 3.7 (60.2%), while ABCI-Inferred with Claude 3.7 reached 66.1%. On the simpler BEQA dataset, ABCI variants achieved ~80% accuracy versus 47-72% for SOTA LLMs. Separating provision retrieval (ReIn) from contextual reasoning improved performance and reduced both overthinking and hallucination problems observed in other variants.
summary.gaps: Existing LLM approaches to legal interpretation of building codes suffer from context loss in RAG, data demands in fine-tuning, and input length limits in prompt engineering; LCW-based contextual reasoning had not previously been explored for legal interpretation of building codes.
summary.future: Validate the framework across diverse LLM architectures and longer context windows, and explore hybrid architectures combining LCW and general-purpose LLMs (inspired by big.LITTLE mobile processor design) or rule-based methods to reduce resource consumption while handling cross-referencing provisions efficiently.

summary.title: State-of-the-Art review of blockchain applications for construction safety: Opportunities, challenges, and future directions
summary.topic: Safety monitoring; Worker monitoring; Quality control; Other
summary.ai_model: Blockchain; Computer vision; Deep learning; Other
summary.abstract: The construction industry remains one of the most hazardous sectors worldwide, facing persistent safety challenges that contribute to high rates of accidents and fatalities. Traditional safety management systems often suffer from inefficiencies, fragmented data handling, and lack of transparency, leading to delays in compliance enforcement and safety monitoring. Blockchain technology, with its decentralized, immutable, and transparent nature, has emerged as a promising solution to enhance construction safety management. This study conducts a systematic review of blockchain applications in construction safety, focusing on their current use cases, benefits, challenges, and future research directions. A systematic literature review (SLR) was conducted using Scopus and Web of Science databases. A total of 14 relevant studies were selected for in-depth qualitative and bibliometric analysis. The findings categorize blockchain applications in construction safety into five research clusters: (i) safety inspections and compliance, (ii) risk and accident information management, (iii) incentive-based safety compliance, (iv) blockchain integration with AI and IoT, and (v) privacy-preserving…
summary.results: Blockchain applications in construction safety cluster into five areas: safety inspections/compliance, risk/accident information management, incentive-based compliance, AI/IoT integration, and privacy-preserving safety monitoring. Blockchain enhances data integrity, automates compliance via smart contracts, incentivizes safe behavior, and supports real-time monitoring, but adoption is hindered by scalability, interoperability, cost, and regulatory uncertainty.
summary.gaps: Existing blockchain research in construction focuses on supply chain, contracts, and procurement, with very limited systematic study of construction safety applications; legal enforceability of smart contracts, regulatory recognition, and standardized governance models for multi-stakeholder safety data are largely unaddressed.
summary.future: Future research should focus on scalable and interoperable blockchain architectures (Layer-2, hybrid models), integration with AI and IoT for smart safety monitoring, privacy-enhancing technologies like zero-knowledge proofs, tokenized incentive mechanisms, and regulatory/legal frameworks for blockchain-based construction safety compliance. Real-world pilot implementations and cross-disciplinary collaborations are also recommended.

summary.title: Enhancing visual-LLM for construction site safety compliance via prompt engineering and Bi-stage retrieval-augmented generation
summary.topic: Safety monitoring; Worker monitoring
summary.ai_model: NLP/LLM; Computer vision; Generative AI; Hybrid
summary.abstract: The escalating frequency of safety incidents on construction sites requires an effective safety management framework. Traditional computer vision systems are constrained by their static nature, limited generalization, and inadequate semantic comprehension. This paper integrates a multi-modal Visual Language Model (VLM) with our proposed Bi-stage Retrieval-Augmented Generation (BiRAG) framework, which enhances safety compliance monitoring based on construction site images, with high scalability and adaptiveness to evolving safety standards without tedious model fine-tuning. A TriPhased prompt (TPP) and a decision-tree-based compliance judgment prompt are designed to enhance the VLM's ability to interpret worker behaviors and safety compliance from site images. A context-aware chunking strategy and hybrid retrieval algorithm are developed to improve the analysis against relevant safety regulations. Experiments with images collected from a real construction site in Hong Kong demonstrated a 7.73 % increase in retrieval accuracy and an 11.66 % improvement in compliance analysis accuracy, offering a holistic construction safety management solution. © 2025
summary.results: The proposed BiRAG framework improved retrieval accuracy by 7.73% and compliance analysis accuracy by 11.66% over a single-stage RAG baseline using InternVL-2 Pro, with similar gains using GPT-4o. Hybrid retrieval (combining dense and sparse methods with reranking) significantly outperformed single-retrieval baselines, and context-aware chunking preserved regulatory semantics. The structured prompting strategies reduced hallucination and enabled scalable, fine-tuning-free adaptation to evolving safety regulations.
summary.gaps: Existing VLMs suffer from hallucinations, poor domain-specific terminology handling, and limited adaptability to regional safety regulation differences; current RAG applications in construction are text-only, rely on dense retrieval, and use inadequate chunking strategies for regulatory documents.
summary.future: Expand the regulatory dataset beyond Hong Kong to include international standards (e.g., OSHA, ISO 45001) for better generalizability. Integrate ontologies or knowledge graphs into the retrieval system to enhance precision and explore more generalized prompting strategies. Evaluate a broader range of VLM architectures and explore optimizations like model quantization for real-time deployment.

summary.title: Exploring Critical Success Factors of AI-Integrated Digital Twins on Saudi Construction Project Deliverables: A PLS-SEM Approach
summary.topic: Cost estimation; Scheduling; Quality control; Safety monitoring; Other
summary.abstract: Artificial intelligence-enhanced digital twins are widely acknowledged as effective instruments for facilitating digital transformation in the building industry. Nonetheless, their implementation remains uneven, with little knowledge regarding the organizational conditions that convert these technologies into enhanced project outcomes. This study investigates the critical success factors (CSFs) that shape the effectiveness of AI-integrated digital twins in Saudi Arabia’s construction industry. A hierarchical structural equation model was developed to capture three dimensions of CSFs, including human-centric, technological, and governance-related, and to evaluate their impact on project deliverables, including time, cost, resource utilization, quality, and risk. Data from a survey of 120 industry professionals were assessed utilizing a PLS-SEM approach, incorporating rigorous measurement and structural assessments. Results indicate that technology and infrastructural factors have the most significant impact on critical success factors, followed by governance and human-related enablers. Consequently, CSFs substantially forecast project outcomes, mediating the influences of all three…
summary.results: Technology/infrastructure factors exert the strongest influence on CSFs (Î²=0.471), followed by governance/standards (Î²=0.414) and human-centric factors (Î²=0.276), with CSFs significantly predicting project deliverables (Î²=0.457, RÂ²â‰ˆ0.21). Mediation analysis confirms that human, technological, and governance enablers affect project deliverables primarily through the CSF construct. Investments in data quality, scalable infrastructure, governance frameworks, and workforce training are essential for successful AI-enabled digital twin adoption.
summary.gaps: Existing models (BIM integration, IoT-DT, AI-DT) address single dimensions in isolation and lack integration of human, technological, and governance factors; validated hierarchical models linking CSFs to measurable project deliverables are absent, and governance and worker-readiness enablers are underexplored.
summary.future: Future research should adopt longitudinal and multilevel designs, integrate objective performance data (cost, schedule, quality records), and conduct cross-country comparative studies. Researchers should also incorporate additional explanatory variables such as procurement strategies, supply chain resilience, and stakeholder collaboration, and perform heterogeneity analyses by role and experience.

summary.title: Semantic BIM enrichment using a hybrid ML and rule-based framework for automated tenement compliance checking
summary.topic: BIM compliance checking; Permitting; Design review
summary.ai_model: Classical ML; Deep learning; Rule-based system; Hybrid
summary.abstract: Semantic enrichment enhances BIM models by extracting structured information, improving their applicability for Automated Code Compliance Checking. Rule-based methods rely on well-defined conditions but struggle with tasks like space classification, where explicit checking rules are unavailable. Meanwhile, ML-based classification introduces adaptability but faces liability challenges due to misclassifications. This paper proposes a hybrid framework integrating ML for space classification and rule-based inferencing for tenement identification. The approach ensures that ML automates preprocessing, improving classification through meticulous feature engineering, while rule-based reasoning guarantees logical consistency during verification. Validated using real-world datasets from residential projects in Mumbai, India as a case, the ML-based space classification component achieves an F1-score of 0.85 and accuracy of 0.86, demonstrating its effectiveness. The deterministic tenement identification process delivers error-free results for various dwelling configurations, making it highly suitable for verification workflows. This study advances scalable BIM-based compliance systems by…
summary.results: The voting ensemble ML model achieved an F1-score of 0.85 and accuracy of 0.86 on space classification, outperforming neural network and GNN (SAGE-E) alternatives, with feature engineering shown to be critical. The rule-based tenement identification produced error-free results across regular and irregular dwelling configurations, and the hybrid pipeline was positively received in a pilot deployment with a Mumbai ULB organization for reducing manual effort and liability risks.
summary.gaps: Prior hybrid approaches focused on parallel ensemble classification rather than sequential ML-preprocessing plus rule-based verification, and existing ACCC systems lack user-in-the-loop verification mechanisms to mitigate ML misclassification liability for urban local bodies.
summary.future: Extend the hybrid framework to other building typologies (commercial, mixed-use) and regional contexts by adapting tenement-space definitions, incorporate higher LOD models with furniture and plumbing fixtures to improve classification, and use Large Language Models and automated feature extraction pipelines to reduce expert effort in feature engineering.

summary.title: Automated analysis of construction safety accident videos using a large multimodal model and graph retrieval-augmented generation
summary.topic: Safety monitoring; Worker monitoring
summary.ai_model: NLP/LLM; Generative AI; Ontology/Knowledge graph; Computer vision; Hybrid
summary.abstract: Safety investigators are challenged by the manual task of analyzing large volumes of accident videos through the repetitive process of reviewing them frame by frame, which is both tedious and labor-intensive. This paper proposes the Accident Video Analysis framework (AcciVid), which automates this process using a large multimodal model (LMM) integrated with Graph Retrieval Augmented Generation (Graph RAG). Accident video content and regulations are converted into Resource Description Framework (RDF) triples and stored as graphs, enabling regulation-based analysis through Graph RAG. AcciVid detected 90 %p more potential safety violations than human safety investigators, achieving an F2 Score of 82.4 % compared to their F2 Score of 54.8 %. Furthermore, AcciVid required only an average of 42 s to generate a draft report, whereas human safety investigators needed an average of 4.6 h. This demonstrates AcciVid's potential as an assistant to safety investigators in reducing manual workloads while maintaining high accuracy and efficiency. © 2025 Elsevier B.V.
summary.results: AcciVid detected 90%p more potential safety violations than human investigators, achieving an F2 score of 82.4% compared to 54.8% for human experts, with higher recall (83.3% vs 50%). The framework generated draft reports in an average of 42 seconds versus 4.6 hours for human investigators, demonstrating substantial efficiency gains while maintaining reasonable precision. The system works best as an assistant to human investigators rather than a replacement, given that 21.1% of its identified violations were disputed by experts.
summary.gaps: Few studies have explored LMM effectiveness in analyzing construction accident videos, and integration of Graph RAG with LMMs for aligning video outputs with precise legal terminology remains underexplored. Prior approaches lack temporal modeling of construction scenes and systematic mechanisms for mapping video insights to structured legal regulations.
summary.future: Future work should incorporate multimodal data sources such as witness interviews, inspection reports, and emergency response documents to enable post-accident inference. The framework should be tested in more visually complex settings with longer-distance footage and extended to other regulatory frameworks like OSHA. Larger validation samples and comparison between real and AI-generated videos are also suggested.

summary.title: Intelligent ESG Evaluation for Construction Enterprises in China: An LLM-Based Model
summary.topic: Other
summary.ai_model: NLP/LLM; Classical ML; Ontology/Knowledge graph; Generative AI
summary.abstract: Environmental, social, and governance (ESG) evaluation has become increasingly critical for company sustainability assessments, especially for enterprises in the construction industry with a high environmental burden. However, existing methods face limitations in subjective evaluation, inconsistent ratings across agencies, and a lack of industry-specificity. To address these limitations, this study proposes a large language model (LLM)-based intelligent ESG evaluation model specifically designed for the construction enterprises in China. The model integrates three modules: (1) an ESG report information extraction module utilizing natural language processing and Chinese pre-trained language models to identify and classify ESG-relevant statements; (2) an ESG rating prediction module employing XGBoost regression with SHAP analysis to predict company ratings and quantify individual statement contributions; and (3) an ESG intelligent evaluation module combining knowledge graph construction with fine-tuned Qwen2.5 language models using Chain-of-Thought (CoT). Empirical validation demonstrates that the model achieves 93.33% accuracy in the ESG rating classification and an R2 score of…
summary.results: The XGBoost-based ESG rating prediction achieved 93.33% classification accuracy and an R2 of 0.5312, with SHAP analysis showing environmental factors contribute most (38.7%), followed by governance (32.0%) and social (29.3%). Integrating a knowledge graph with the fine-tuned LLM improved evaluation accuracy from 53.33% to 65%, a 21.88% relative improvement, also enhancing output consistency.
summary.gaps: Existing ESG research lacks systematic, sentence-level evaluation mechanisms for individual company reports to guide internal ESG improvement, and rating agencies show significant inconsistency and limited industry-specificity for construction enterprises.
summary.future: The authors suggest expanding data sources beyond self-reported disclosures to include news, regulatory filings, audits, sensor and supply chain data; refining predictive accuracy and dynamic adaptation to evolving policies; and integrating the model with enterprise management systems to close the loop from assessment to corrective action. They also propose extending the framework to other industries and incorporating multi-modal data.

summary.title: GPT Applications for Construction Safety: A Use Case Analysis
summary.topic: Safety monitoring; Worker monitoring; Other
summary.abstract: This study explores the use of Large Language Models (LLMs), specifically GPT, for different safety management applications in the construction industry. Many studies have explored the integration of GPT in construction safety for various applications; their primary focus has been on the feasibility of such integration, often using GPT models for specific applications rather than a thorough evaluation of GPT’s limitations and capabilities. In contrast, this study aims to provide a comprehensive assessment of GPT’s performance based on established key criteria. Using structured use cases, this study explores GPT’s strength and weaknesses in four construction safety areas: (1) delivering personalized safety training and educational content tailored to individual learner needs; (2) automatically analyzing post-accident reports to identify root causes and suggest preventive measures; (3) generating customized safety guidelines and checklists to support site compliance; and (4) providing real-time assistance for managing daily safety tasks and decision-making on construction sites. LLMs and NLP have already been employed in each of these four areas for improvement, making them suitable…
summary.results: GPT demonstrated acceptable performance in delivering evidence-based, OSHA-aligned responses across training, accident analysis, guideline generation, and real-time assistance tasks. However, it showed significant limitations in deeper critical analysis, extrapolation beyond explicit information, adapting to dynamic site conditions, and providing consistent human-like empathetic responses. The authors conclude GPT requires fine-tuning, real-time data integration, and human oversight before reliable deployment in safety-critical contexts.
summary.gaps: No systematic evaluation exists of LLM role in construction safety management; prior work focuses on feasibility or isolated applications without assessing breadth and depth of LLM capabilities across multiple safety functions, nor their alignment with regulatory standards and contextual demands.
summary.future: Future work should fine-tune GPT with safety-specific documents, integrate real-time site data for contextual awareness, evaluate other LLMs beyond GPT, develop multiple scenarios per use case, incorporate safety professional feedback, and conduct longitudinal studies and real-world implementation trials to assess sustained utility and impact.

summary.title: Beyond Development: Challenges in Deploying Machine-Learning Models for Structural Engineering Applications
summary.topic: Structural design; Quality control
summary.abstract: Machine learning (ML) solutions are rapidly changing the landscape of many fields, including structural engineering. Despite their promising performance, these approaches are usually only demonstrated as proofs of concept in structural engineering, and are rarely deployed for real-world applications. This paper illustrates the challenges of developing ML models suitable for deployment with a focus on generalizability and explainability. Among various pitfalls, the paper discusses the impact of model overfitting, underfitting, and underspecification, training data non-representativeness, variable omission bias, and possible shortcomings of conventional cross-validation and feature importance-based explainability for correlated random variables. Two structural engineering-specific illustrative examples highlight the importance of implementing rigorous model validation techniques through adaptive sampling, careful physics-informed feature selection, and considerations of both model complexity and generalizability. © 2025 American Society of Civil Engineers.
summary.results: Traditional accuracy metrics and cross-validation can mask serious generalizability problems, as shown by random forest models outperforming linear models under standard cross-validation but failing under adaptive cross-validation that tests new parameter combinations. Omission of physically important features leads to overfitting that cannot be compensated by adding other features, and permutation-based feature importance can mislead users when features are correlated or models are underspecified. Simpler, physics-informed models often generalize better and are more trustworthy for deployment than complex black-box models.
summary.gaps: Little attention has been paid in structural engineering to ML model deployment beyond proof-of-concept, and no systematic treatment exists of generalizability failures, underspecification, and limitations of feature-importanceâ€“based explainability in this domain.
summary.future: The paper calls for better validation practices including stratified/adaptive cross-validation, continuous local validation borrowed from MLOps, and stress testing with shifted evaluation sets. It also recommends reducing model complexity, integrating engineering intuition and physical knowledge into feature selection, and improving explainability beyond feature-importance metrics. Open sharing of code and data to support reproducibility is encouraged.

summary.title: Achieving Sustainable Construction Safety Management: The Shift from Compliance to Intelligence via BIM–AI Convergence
summary.topic: Safety monitoring; Worker monitoring; Quality control
summary.ai_model: Deep learning; Classical ML; Computer vision; Digital twin; Hybrid
summary.abstract: Traditional construction safety management, reliant on manual inspections and heuristic judgments, increasingly fails to address the dynamic, multi-dimensional risks of modern projects, perpetuating fragmented safety governance and reactive hazard mitigation. This study proposes an integrated building information modeling (BIM)–AI platform to unify safety supervision across the project lifecycle, synthesizing spatial-temporal data from BIM with AI-driven probabilistic models and IoT-enabled real-time monitoring for sustainable construction safety management. Employing a Design Science Research methodology, the platform’s phase-agnostic architecture bridges technical–organizational divides, while the Multilayer Neural Risk Coupling Assessment framework quantifies interdependencies among structural, environmental, and human risk factors. Prototype testing in real-world projects demonstrates improved risk detection accuracy, reduced reliance on manual processes, and enhanced cross-departmental collaboration. The system transitions safety regimes from compliance-based protocols to proactive, data-empowered governance. This approach offers scalability across diverse projects. The…
summary.results: The prototype BIM-AI platform, validated in regional pilot projects, effectively transitioned safety management from reactive to proactive governance, helping avoid major safety accidents during construction cycles. Users rated the system positively (mean 4.1/5) on information friendliness, risk warning timeliness, inspection optimization, and safety improvement. The MNRA framework successfully quantified interdependencies among structural, environmental, and human risk factors across the project lifecycle.
summary.gaps: The paper identifies three gaps in prior literature: phase fragmentation in BIM-AI implementations, organizational decoupling between technical advancements and managerial workflows, and a proactive governance deficit favoring real-time detection over upstream prevention.
summary.future: Future work should expand adaptability to low-resource environments via edge computing and lightweight AI models, develop hybrid human-AI intelligence frameworks with explainable AI interfaces to mitigate organizational resistance, and conduct longitudinal studies across diverse project types (underground engineering, smart cities). Integration with digital twins and blockchain-enabled safety traceability systems is also proposed.

summary.title: How can corporate digital responsibility (CDR) be measured in line with corporate social responsibility (CSR)? A new theoretical approach in construction 4.0
summary.topic: Safety monitoring; Scheduling; Cost estimation; Quality control; Design review; Other
summary.abstract: Corporate responsibility in Civil Engineering in the digital era is changing rapidly. An attempt is made to make CDR more “tangible” by assigning and defining entrepreneurial approaches. This paper investigates the relationship between CSR and CDR based on a structured literature analysis, Internet research and Hermeneutic approach. The study examines the status quo of existing methods for measuring CDR and proposes a practicable framework for measuring successfully practiced CDR. The paper investigates the value-based use of digitization and Artificial Intelligence (AI) as crucial factors to derive new ways to shape and catalyze the industry's assumption of human, social and environmental responsibility. The study defines a new approach to a corporate strategy in order to make the fulfillment of CSR measurable and assessable with regard to the effects of digital technological innovations on human, society and environment, taking into account current Environmental, Social, and Governance (ESG) regulations and guidelines. © 2024 ERP Environment and John Wiley & Sons Ltd.
summary.results: The study concludes that CDR differs from CSR by explicitly centering technology's impact on humans, society, and environment, and proposes that CDR can be measured through ESG scores, KPIs, and CSV metrics. Empirical vignettes from three companies demonstrate that responsible digitization yields measurable benefits including efficiency gains, CO2 reduction (up to ~20%), improved safety, employee identification, and competitive advantage. A CDR-integrated reporting approach enhances transparency of intangible corporate assets and investor trust.
summary.gaps: No internationally valid framework exists for measuring CDR; construction lacks empirical data, legal frameworks for AI, cross-mapping between CSR and CDR, and standardized KPIs for assessing corporate digital responsibility's effectiveness.
summary.future: Future research should generate quantitative empirical data to test the conceptual CDR measurement model and scale, develop measurement formulas and benchmark values, and extend the model to examine effects on trust, innovation willingness, investment intention, and sustainability performance. Deeper interdisciplinary research combining engineering, IT, HR, and corporate development is needed to operationalize CDR metrics.

summary.title: Achieving On-Site Trustworthy AI Implementation in the Construction Industry: A Framework Across the AI Lifecycle
summary.topic: Safety monitoring; Worker monitoring; Scheduling; Quality control; Design review; Other
summary.ai_model: Computer vision; NLP/LLM; Deep learning; Blockchain; Other
summary.abstract: In recent years, the application of artificial intelligence (AI) technology in the construction industry has rapidly emerged, particularly in areas such as site monitoring and project management. This technology has demonstrated its great potential in enhancing safety and productivity in construction. However, concerns regarding the technical maturity and reliability, safety, and privacy implications have led to a lack of trust in AI among stakeholders and end users in the construction industry, which slows the intelligent transformation of the industry, particularly for on-site AI implementation. This paper reviews frameworks for AI system design across various sectors and government regulations and requirements for achieving trustworthy and responsible AI. The principles for the AI system design are then determined. Furthermore, a lifecycle design framework specifically tailored for AI systems deployed in the construction industry is proposed. This framework addresses six key phases, including planning, data collection, algorithm development, deployment, maintenance, and archiving, and clarifies the design principles and development priorities needed for each phase to enhance AI…
summary.results: The authors identify 13 principles for trustworthy AI organized into internal characteristics, interaction principles, and social impact, derived from cross-sector reviews and government guidelines. They propose an operational framework mapping these principles to six lifecycle phases, highlighting construction-specific concerns such as on-site hardware security, worker privacy, data scarcity, and environmental impact. The framework provides design guidance to enhance AI acceptance in on-site construction applications.
summary.gaps: Most construction AI research remains at proof-of-concept stage without widespread adoption, and there is a lack of frameworks addressing trustworthiness across the entire AI lifecycle specifically for on-site construction implementation.
summary.future: Extend the framework to cover planning, design, and maintenance phases of the building lifecycle beyond on-site construction, including LLM-based applications for BIM retrieval, compliance checking, and scheduling. Develop practical implementation approaches tailored to specific AI technologies and tasks, and build a more comprehensive lifecycle framework.

summary.title: AI integration in architectural design and management: professionals’ perspectives
summary.topic: Design review; BIM compliance checking; Contract management; Other
summary.abstract: Artificial Intelligence (AI) is reshaping industries through increased efficiency, cost reduction, and time savings, yet its adoption in the built environment, particularly in Architectural Design Management (ADM), remains limited. This study investigates current practices, challenges, and opportunities related to AI integration in ADM. Using a qualitative approach, 23 semi-structured interviews were conducted with experienced professionals across diverse regions. While all participants were aware of AI, 83% reported using it in daily practice, primarily for design iteration, optimisation, brief compliance, parametric workflows, and creative enhancement. Key challenges identified include legal uncertainty, sector standardisation, reliability, and ethical concerns. Future opportunities were also noted, such as AI support in administrative tasks, document review, coordination, and job creation. The findings are synthesised into a SWOT-TAM framework, aligned with perceived usefulness and ease of use, offering valuable insights for guiding effective and responsible AI adoption in ADM. © 2025 The Author(s). Published by Informa UK Limited, trading as Taylor & Francis Group.
summary.results: While all 23 participants were aware of AI and 83% use it in daily practice (primarily for design iteration, optimization, brief compliance, parametric workflows, and creative enhancement), AI adoption in ADM is confined to discrete tasks rather than integrated across the design lifecycle. Key challenges include legal uncertainty around liability and ownership, lack of sector standardization, reliability/security concerns, and ethical/psychosocial impacts. Opportunities include administrative task automation, document review, multidisciplinary coordination, and emerging roles such as AI Educator and Curator.
summary.gaps: Limited research exists on AI adoption impacts in architectural design (as opposed to construction project management), and there is a lack of in-depth interview studies exploring design team perspectives on AI integration. Additionally, no prior work integrates SWOT strategic analysis with TAM behavioral insights to guide AI adoption in ADM.
summary.future: Future research should empirically validate the SWOT-TAM model and assess the relative influence of each element on actual system use. Longitudinal studies are needed to evaluate the sustained impact of AI on design quality, professional identity, and sector resilience.

summary.title: Collaborative Governance: Blockchain-Based Federated Learning for Construction Safety Service
summary.topic: Safety monitoring; Worker monitoring
summary.abstract: Deep learning (DL) models are increasingly used to identify unsafe activities for the construction safety service (CSS). However, two typical issues threaten DL training process performance: poor security and privacy in data sharing. To address these problems, a blockchain-based federated learning (BCFL) framework is proposed from a collaborative governance perspective to obtain optimistic DL models for CSS. Two special works of this BCFL framework are that 1) it develops the federated learning empowered privacy-preserving data sharing with the principle of sharing data model weights instead of raw data (especially for one DL application for CSS, the Fed-YOLOv4 model for workers' unsafe behavior identification task is developed) and 2) it explores two blockchain-based secure model sharing strategies that involve blockchain-interplanetary file system combination and model training contribution computing. Then, the smart contracts are further developed with the strategies above to streamline the workflow of federated DL model training. Finally, we apply the proposed framework to the practical subway project. The results demonstrate that the proposed framework can improve the DL…
summary.results: The Fed-YOLOv4 model aggregated from 4 clients improved mAP by 20.97% over the non-federated YOLOv4 model for worker unsafe behavior identification, demonstrating that federated learning can achieve better accuracy without compromising privacy. Smart contract deployment costs were low (approximately 168-213 RMB per contract), confirming economic feasibility for practical application among construction organizations.
summary.gaps: Prevailing solutions focus on data security using blockchain but ignore data privacy in construction; BCFL has not been applied to construction safety with integrated security and privacy considerations, and workflows for federated DL training within blockchain networks remain unexplored.
summary.future: Future work should apply the BCFL framework to other CSS applications beyond worker unsafe behavior identification to verify broader effectiveness. Research is also needed on off-chain data security using cryptographic techniques (differential privacy, homomorphic encryption), smart contracts, and IoT integration to prevent fraudulent data uploads.

summary.title: Responsible AI in structural engineering: a framework for ethical use
summary.topic: Structural design; Safety monitoring; Quality control; Facility management; Design review; Other
summary.ai_model: Classical ML; Deep learning; Computer vision; Digital twin; Other
summary.abstract: The integration of Artificial Intelligence (AI) into structural engineering holds great promise for advancing analysis, design, and maintenance. However, it also raises critical ethical and governance challenges—including bias, lack of transparency, accountability gaps, and equity concerns—which are particularly significant in a discipline where public safety is paramount. This study addresses these issues through eight fictional but realistic case studies that illustrate plausible ethical dilemmas, such as algorithmic bias in predictive models and tensions between AI-generated recommendations and human engineering judgment. In response, the study proposes a structured framework for responsible AI implementation, organized into three key domains: (i) Technical Foundations (focusing on bias mitigation, robust validation, and explainability); (ii) Operational and Governance Considerations (emphasizing industry standards and human-in-the-loop oversight); and (iii) Professional and Societal Responsibilities (advocating for equity, accessibility, and ethical awareness among engineers). The framework offers actionable guidance for engineers, policymakers, and researchers seeking to…
summary.results: The paper concludes that ethical AI integration in structural engineering requires addressing bias, explainability, validation, human oversight, and equity through an interconnected framework rather than isolated measures. It emphasizes shared accountability across the AI lifecycle among engineers, developers, and institutions, and argues that ethical frameworks must remain adaptable to regional regulatory and cultural differences.
summary.gaps: The paper identifies a significant gap in literature addressing ethical considerations specific to AI in structural engineering, as well as a lack of systematic validation methodologies, lifecycle governance frameworks, and regionally adaptable ethical standards for the field.
summary.future: The authors call for interdisciplinary research on AI validation and uncertainty quantification, reform of engineering education to integrate AI ethics, adaptation to emerging technologies like quantum computing and digital twins, development of lifecycle oversight and sunset policies, and more inclusive AI deployment strategies for underserved communities.

summary.title: A platform-based Natural Language processing-driven strategy for digitalising regulatory compliance processes for the built environment
summary.topic: BIM compliance checking; Permitting; Design review
summary.ai_model: NLP/LLM; Ontology/Knowledge graph; Deep learning; Hybrid
summary.abstract: The digitalisation of the regulatory compliance process has been an active area of research for several decades. However, more recently the level of activities in this area has increased considerably. In the UK, the tragic incident of Grenfell fire in 2017 has been a major catalyst for this as a result of the Hackitt report's recommendations pointing a lot of the blame on the broken regulatory regime in the country. The Hackitt report emphasises the need to overhaul the building regulations, but the approach to do so remains an open research question. Existing work in this space tends to overlook the processing of actual regulatory documents, or limits their scope to solving a relatively small subtask. This paper presents a new comprehensive platform approach to the digitalisation of the regulatory compliance processing. We present i-ReC (intelligent Regulatory Compliance), a platform approach to digitalisation of regulatory compliance that takes into consideration the enormous diversity of all the stakeholders’ activities. A historical perspective on research in this area is first presented to put things in perspective which identifies the challenges in such an endeavour and…
summary.results: The authors demonstrate that semi-automated semantic enrichment of building regulations is feasible and improves identification of documents and sections dealing with specific topics. Their SPaR.txt tool for multi-word expression identification and passage-retrieval IR system outperformed comparable commercial engines (including BSOL) on all objective criteria across 42 queries, retrieving relevant top-3 results for 35 of 42 queries. They also show that fully automated end-to-end ACC is likely impossible (AI-hard) because many performance-based regulations contain hidden ambiguities, and that human responsibility/accountability cannot be delegated to a computer.
summary.gaps: Gaps include lack of standardised approaches to modelling and aggregating rules, absence of transparency in compliance assessments, limited coverage of BIM labels versus regulatory terminology, licensing restrictions preventing data sharing, and the absence of FAIR principles in AEC IR research where code and data are rarely publicly available.
summary.future: Improving SPaR.txt performance with larger and more diverse training datasets, developing entity linking and coreference resolution across sentence boundaries, creating aligned strategies to collect comprehensive domain vocabularies in a knowledge graph, and developing tools to support integration of new terminology. Future IR work should expand dataset size and test additional document expansion approaches, while more effort is needed on cleaning processed regulatory texts.

summary.title: Deep neural networks for corporate misconduct prediction in construction industry using data from social networks
summary.topic: Other
summary.abstract: Given the complex and continually adapting nature of misconduct, this study aims to update and interpret a misconduct prediction model using the latest techniques, i.e., deep neural networks (DNN) and social network information for Chinese construction companies. Social networks have been reported as drivers of corruption in the construction industry; however, such networks are seldom included as inputs in existing models. Based on data from 119 listed Chinese construction firms, this study applied a DNN to construct a corporate misconduct prediction model. The inputs of this model included variables related to corporate governance and financial performance, as examined in previous studies, but also social network information. This study found that the DNN demonstrated superior performance compared to benchmark models. To interpret the constructed model further and assess the role of social networks in predictions, this study also employed SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP), which could calculate the importance of each variable. The 20 most influential variables were identified, almost 50% of which were related to social networks. The findings indicate that the proposed model…
summary.results: The DNN model outperformed LR, SVM, KNN, DT, XGBoost, and RF benchmarks with 83.25% accuracy in predicting corporate misconduct for Chinese construction firms. SHAP analysis showed that 9 of the top 20 most influential features were social network-related variables, confirming that social networks play a central role in misconduct alongside corporate governance and financial performance.
summary.gaps: Prior misconduct prediction models rarely include social network information and lack interpretability, and deep learning has not been applied to misconduct prediction in Chinese construction firms.
summary.future: Future work should explore the underlying positive and negative mechanisms of social networks on misconduct, incorporate textual information from annual reports, test generalizability to other industries and regions (especially East Asian guanxi cultures), and optimize the DNN with more complex architectures.

summary.title: Assessing Trust in Construction AI-Powered Collaborative Robots Using Structural Equation Modeling
summary.topic: Worker monitoring; Safety monitoring; Quality control; Other
summary.abstract: This study aimed to investigate the key technical and psychological factors that impact the architecture, engineering, and construction (AEC) professionals' trust in collaborative robots (cobots) powered by artificial intelligence (AI). This study seeks to address the critical knowledge gaps surrounding the establishment and reinforcement of trust among AEC professionals in their collaboration with AI-powered cobots. In the context of the construction industry, where the complexities of tasks often necessitate human-robot teamwork, understanding the technical and psychological factors influencing trust is paramount. Such trust dynamics play a pivotal role in determining the effectiveness of human-robot collaboration on construction sites. This research employed a nationwide survey of 600 AEC industry practitioners to shed light on these influential factors, providing valuable insights to calibrate trust levels and facilitate the seamless integration of AI-powered cobots into the AEC industry. Additionally, it aimed to gather insights into opportunities for promoting the adoption, cultivation, and training of a skilled workforce to effectively leverage this technology. A structural…
summary.results: Safety and reliability emerged as the most significant factors for cobot adoption in construction, with training and robustness directly influencing safety perception. Transparency of cobot decision-making positively affects accuracy, robustness, security, privacy, and communication, which in turn support higher levels of automation and trust. Workers expressed hesitancy toward fully autonomous cobots, preferring human supervision, and emphasized the importance of hands-on experience, peer recommendations, and comprehensive training.
summary.gaps: Limited research on cobots specifically in construction (versus manufacturing), absence of worker/end-user perspectives in trust research, and lack of empirical validation of trust dimensions in real-world construction deployments.
summary.future: The authors recommend longitudinal, experimental studies using real or simulated cobots to establish causal directions and assess trust calibration over time, including physiological measurement of trust. They also suggest differentiating perceptions across professional roles (laborers, managers, engineers) and examining how project type and size influence trust dynamics.

summary.title: A Systematic Review of the Socio-Legal Dimensions of Responsible AI and Its Role in Improving Health and Safety in Construction
summary.topic: Safety monitoring; Worker monitoring; Design review; Scheduling
summary.ai_model: Generative AI; Computer vision; Digital twin; Other
summary.abstract: Integrating artificial intelligence (AI) in the construction industry could revolutionise workplace safety and efficiency. However, this integration also carries complex socio-legal implications that require further investigation. Presently, there is a research gap in the socio-legal dimensions of AI use to enhance health and safety regulations and protocols for the construction sector in the United Kingdom, particularly in understanding how the existing legal frameworks can adapt to AI integration effectively. Comprehensive research is indispensable to identify where the existing regulations may fall short or require more specificity in addressing the unique implications introduced by AI technologies. This article aims to address the pressing socio-legal challenges surrounding the integration of AI in the UK construction industry, specifically in enhancing health and safety protocols on construction sites, through a systematic review encompassing the PRISMA protocol. The review has identified that the existing legal and regulatory framework provides a strong foundation for risk management. Still, it needs to sufficiently account for the socio-legal dimensions introduced by AI…
summary.results: The existing UK legal and regulatory framework provides a strong foundation for risk management but does not sufficiently account for socio-legal dimensions introduced by AI deployment or anticipate how AI may evolve. The HSE needs standardised authorities, additional resources, and empowerment to effectively oversee AI in construction, including conducting technical, empirical, and governance audits. Legal responsibility for AI actions currently remains with humans, and establishing AI legal personhood would require profound legal, ethical, and technological changes.
