summary.gaps: There is a lack of research on the socio-legal dimensions of AI integration in UK construction health and safety, and no systematic understanding of how existing legal frameworks can adapt to AI, particularly regarding liability, bias, data privacy, and regulatory compliance specific to construction.
summary.future: Future studies should evaluate ongoing UK legislative efforts, including the Artificial Intelligence (Regulation) Bill and forthcoming stage-two guidance, to assess their adequacy in addressing AI deployment in construction safety. Research should also explore the viability of AI legal personhood and the development of specific regulatory frameworks for autonomous AI decision-making in safety-critical contexts.

summary.title: Multidimensional evolutionary analysis of China’s BIM technology policy based on quantitative mapping
summary.topic: BIM compliance checking; Other
summary.abstract: In the wave of the digital era, Building Information Modelling (BIM) has emerged as the primary tool for intelligent construction and digital transformation in the Architecture, Engineering, and Construction (AEC) industry. China's focus on policy guidance for the dissemination and application of BIM technology has promoted high-quality development and technological innovation in the AEC industry. However, few studies have described the multi-dimensional evolution picture of BIM technology policy in China, and lack of effective grasp and prediction of policy evolution law and future direction. An improved policy quantitative analysis framework is built using natural language processing (NLP) based on deep learning in this paper. The dynamic characteristics of 242 Chinese BIM technology policy documents from 1998 to 2022 in the PKULAW database are quantitatively analyzed by the framework, and the four-stage integrated evolution of Chinese BIM technology policy is quantitatively mapped in a visual form through network analysis and dynamic topic model (DTM). Furthermore, this research conducts a comprehensive discussion from three dimensions, providing valuable insights for policy…
summary.results: China's BIM technology policy evolved through four stages (1998-2010, 2011-2014, 2015-2018, 2019-2022), shifting from single-department issuance by the Ministry of Housing and Urban-Rural Development toward multi-department collaboration after 2019, with two distinct cooperative clusters emerging around traditional construction and transportation/infrastructure. Policy targets cycled through 'industry transformation', 'technology development', and 'practical application', with target iteration accelerating and themes becoming more diverse and interconnected after BIM's formal introduction in 2011. Core policy themes have shifted toward quality management, big data development, intelligent equipment, and transportation applications, reflecting a move from conservative to transformative…
summary.gaps: The study focuses on central-level policies and lacks consideration of regional heterogeneity, and it does not quantitatively analyze the interaction between BIM policy development and AEC industry performance.
summary.future: Future BIM policy is expected to expand into transportation facility applications, engineering quality management, prefabricated building adoption, and construction industry big data platforms. The authors also call for further research on regional heterogeneity beyond central-level policy and on the interaction mechanism between BIM policy development and AEC industry performance.

summary.title: LEVERAGING LARGE LANGUAGE MODELS FOR ENHANCED CONSTRUCTION SAFETY REGULATION EXTRACTION
summary.topic: Safety monitoring; Other
summary.abstract: SUMMARY: The construction sector has long been known for its complicated safety requirements, which are critical to ensure the well-being of workers on site. However, interpreting these requirements and maintaining compliance can be difficult due to the amount and complexity of the paperwork involved. This leads to difficulty extracting safety information from requirement documents. Besides, information that is presented in a manner similar to human-like responses can improve employee understanding. This study proposed a Construction Safety Query Assistant (CSQA) approach to enhance the extraction and knowledge of construction safety regulations using Large Language Models (LLMs). CSQA comprises of three primary components: (1) the Construction Safety Investigation Module (CSI), which gathers and processes safety regulation documents through text extraction and preprocessing to build a searchable database; (2) the Safety Condition Identification Module (SCI), which utilizes LLMs to interpret user queries and extract relevant information from the CSI database, capitalizing on the models' ability to understand context and subtle textual nuances; and (3) the Safety Information…
summary.results: The CSQA prototype successfully retrieved contextually relevant safety information from OSHA documents for ladder and scaffold scenarios, and user evaluation showed positive mean scores across learnability (3.8), interaction (4.5), communication (4.1), and relevancy (4.4) on a 5-point Likert scale. The system demonstrated that LLMs with RAG can support safety managers and construction students in accessing and understanding regulatory requirements more efficiently than manual review.
summary.gaps: The study identifies limited empirical research on automatically extracting requirements from construction safety rules for field compliance, lack of evaluation of hallucination risks in LLM-based safety systems, and narrow case scope limited to scaffolding and ladders.
summary.future: Expand CSQA to cover a broader range of safety regulations and practical applications, implement continuous feedback loops to address hallucinations and improve robustness, investigate algorithm precision in information retrieval, and integrate the approach with other safety processes such as Job Hazard Analysis and safety training.

summary.title: Novel blockchain deep learning framework to ensure video security and lightweight storage for construction safety management
summary.topic: Safety monitoring; Worker monitoring
summary.abstract: In construction management, video data tampering behavior like manual forging and deletion can negatively impact on-site safety and accident accountability. Blockchain technology holds the potential to address this issue by leveraging distributed ledger characteristics. However, blockchain's limited storage capacity and block size make it difficult to upload large-sized construction data such as daily monitoring video. Furthermore, it is unnecessary to store all construction data in any case. Therefore, this study proposes a blockchain deep learning framework that focuses on how to efficiently extract and securely store key information (i.e., video summarization that involves worker's unsafe behavior) on-blockchain for data traceability. The framework involves a novel data-driven and rule-based keyframe extraction (DRKE) model to lightweight large-sized construction video in the nascent field of deep learning and blockchain combination. To define parameters for the DRKE model, specific construction rules (e.g., people's unsafe behavior-based and people-based rules) have been pre-defined. This framework has been evaluated, and the results demonstrate its capability for effective…
summary.results: The proposed DRKE model achieved mAPs of 67.00% and 75.18% on two datasets and reduced video memory usage by an average of 78.14% through keyframe extraction. The blockchain simulation demonstrated that tampering with stored keyframes is detectable via hash mismatch, confirming data immutability. Integrating deep learning-based keyframe extraction with on-chain/off-chain (IPFS) storage effectively resolves blockchain's storage limitation while preserving video integrity for accident accountability.
summary.gaps: Limited prior studies have explored how blockchain manages large-sized construction video data, and existing feature-based keyframe extraction methods lack flexibility and interpretability for construction management needs.
summary.future: Future work should improve DRKE model mAP by increasing training data via customized privacy-preserving smart contracts, extend the approach to other types of unsafe behavior and construction systems, and perform practical evaluations of blockchain performance (latency, throughput) in deployed prototypes. The authors also propose extending the framework to industry-level federated learning across multiple construction projects.

summary.title: Competencies for Human-Robot Collaboration in the Construction Industry–Academia’s Perspective
summary.topic: Worker monitoring; Safety monitoring; Quality control; Other
summary.abstract: This paper investigates the perceptions of Construction Engineering and Management instructors regarding the competencies for Human-Robot Collaboration (HRC) in construction to determine knowledge areas, skills, and abilities prioritized for facilitating effective collaboration between humans and robots in the industry. A two-round Delphi study was employed to evaluate the perceptions of construction instructors regarding HRC competencies. This study’s findings revealed that human-robot collaboration knowledge areas prioritized by the instructors include HRC ethics and regulation, robot anatomy and technical specifications, construction robot applications, sensors, and task planning. The instructors prioritized skills such as task planning, application of machine learning algorithms, safety management, human-robot interface proficiency, and effective communication. HRC abilities prioritized include decision-making, continuous learning, critical thinking, attention to detail, analytical aptitude, and adaptability. This research established the competencies prioritized by the instructors for implementing HRC in the construction industry and recommended future research directions. ©…
summary.results: Instructors prioritized HRC knowledge areas including ethics and regulation, robot anatomy, construction robot applications, sensors, and task planning; key skills included task planning, machine learning application, safety management, human-robot interface proficiency, and communication; and core abilities included decision-making, continuous learning, critical thinking, attention to detail, analytical aptitude, and adaptability. Consensus was reached among the expert panel (SD within 0â€“1.5) with high Cronbach's alpha reliability (0.91â€“0.96), indicating broad agreement that CEM curricula should be revised to incorporate these HRC competencies.
summary.gaps: The paper identifies a gap in understanding what competencies (knowledge, skills, abilities) construction workers need for safe and effective collaboration with robots, and a lack of HRC-focused content in current CEM curricula.
summary.future: Future research should investigate construction industry practitioners' perceptions of HRC competencies to complement the academic view, and explore which pedagogical approaches (active, experiential, collaborative learning) best equip students with these competencies.

summary.title: Blockchain-Based Onsite Activity Management for Smart Construction Process Quality Traceability
summary.topic: Quality control; Worker monitoring
summary.abstract: Onsite construction activities (OCAs) are essential components affecting construction process quality. Tracing OCAs can control the construction process with high-resolution visibility, help stakeholders demonstrate their compliance with regulations, and reduce interorganizational quality disputes. Traditional technologies cannot meet the information recording demands for traceability, namely, immutability, transparency, and auditability. This work introduces a novel framework for the traceability of OCAs based on computer vision and blockchain technologies. First, cutting-edge deep learning algorithms are introduced to automatically extract OCA information from far-field surveillance videos. Second, a consortium blockchain system is built to record the identified OCA information and the hash value of the raw data for future review. Finally, a case of a high-rise office construction project is used to test and verify the feasibility of the framework, in which a blockchain prototype is developed based on a Blockchain as a Service (BaaS) platform, termly, PolyChain. The experimental results show that the BaaS-based prototype is an effective system architecture with good throughput…
summary.results: The proposed blockchain-and-computer-vision framework can automatically extract worker activity information from far-field surveillance videos and record it together with hashes of raw video in a consortium blockchain, ensuring immutability and traceability. Experimental evaluation of the PolyChain-based prototype achieved throughput of around 750 TPS and maximum latency of 3 seconds with 10 nodes, indicating acceptable performance for construction applications. The approach enhances visibility of construction processes and provides a reliable basis for quality accountability and dispute reduction.
summary.gaps: Existing research has focused on blockchain for supply chains or inspection texts but has not addressed traceability of onsite construction activities, and blockchain-as-a-service solutions remain largely unexplored in the construction industry.
summary.future: Future work should integrate multiple sensing technologies (e.g., RFID, GPS, LiDAR, millimeter-wave radar) to collect richer quality information including worker identity and location for traceability. Smart contracts should be extended to automatically check compliance of construction procedures against quality regulations during specific periods. Empirical benefit-cost analyses from pilot projects are needed to validate practical adoption.

summary.title: Corporate digital responsibility (CDR) in construction engineering—ethical guidelines for the application of digital transformation and artificial intelligence (AI) in user practice
summary.topic: BIM compliance checking; Quality control; Safety monitoring; Facility management; Design review; Scheduling; Cost estimation; Other
summary.ai_model: Digital twin; Computer vision; Deep learning; Classical ML; Other
summary.abstract: Digitization is developing fast and has become a powerful tool for digital planning, construction and operations, for instance digital twins. Now is the right time for constructive approaches and to apply ethics-by-design in order to develop and implement a safe and efficient artificial intelligence (AI) application. So far, no study has addressed the key research question: Where can corporate digital responsibility (CDR) be allocated, and how shall an adequate ethical framework be designed to support digital innovations in order to make full use of the potentials of digitization and AI? Therefore, the research on how best practices meet their corporate responsibility in the digital transformation process and the requirements of the EU for trustworthy AI and its human-friendly use is essential. Its transformation bears a high potential for companies, is critical for success and thus, requires responsible handling. This study generates data by conducting case studies and interviewing experts as part of the qualitative method to win profound insights into applied practice. It provides an assessment of demands stated in the Sustainable Development Goals by the United Nations (SDGs),…
summary.results: CDR with ethical principles is identified as the key driver for success, efficiency, and sustainability in applying digitization and AI in construction engineering. The study finds that self-commitment is insufficient and that binding legal standards, interdisciplinary academic training, explainable AI, and diversity are needed; innovative companies with value-based cultures outperform conservative ones. Case studies (PERI, Wayss & Freytag, APLEONA) demonstrate that data ownership, data protection, education, and human-centered design are practical barriers requiring ethical and regulatory clarification.
summary.gaps: No prior study has conceptualized CDR in construction engineering in relation to digitization and AI, and related literature (unlike in medicine, automotive, or philosophy) is missing in construction. Ethical principles, diversity considerations, and standards for human-led AI in the construction industry are underdeveloped.
summary.future: Future research should further develop interdisciplinary ethical frameworks for AI in construction, adapt engineering academic curricula to include technical ethics, and conduct follow-up longitudinal surveys to monitor human-technology relationships. The author calls for expanded investigation into CDR implementation in SMEs, binding European ethical standards for AI, and cross-sector learning to strengthen trustworthy AI 'Made in Germany'.

summary.title: Towards a responsible integration of artificial intelligence technology in the construction sector
summary.topic: Safety monitoring; Scheduling; Cost estimation; Design review; Worker monitoring; Contract management; Quality control; Other
summary.ai_model: Classical ML; Deep learning; Rule-based system; Other
summary.abstract: The uptake of artificial intelligence (AI) innovations in the construction industry implies new physical and socio-political risks. Risk analysis is crucial to managing these risks, but is challenging due to the inherent complexity and lack of applied knowledge specific to construction activities. We forecast potential AI innovation trends related to construction from a keyword concurrence analysis of 974 journal articles. We use this analysis to identify potential sector-specific risks in construction activities by forming a risk map based on an analysis of ninety-four articles related to the ethics and impacts of AI technologies. We found that trends in innovation more often involve areas in construction considered 'back-end' tasks, as opposed to 'on-site'. Thus, the potential risks and regulatory challenges from the use of AI technology in the construction sector will be legal, financial, and social, as opposed to risks involving physical harm to users on construction sites. © The Author(s) 2021.
summary.results: AI innovation in construction is shifting from 'front-end' physical tasks to 'back-end' tasks like planning, design, and decision-making, meaning future risks will be primarily legal, financial, and social rather than physical harm on sites. Six overlapping risk categories emerge (unemployment, occupational segregation, accidents, privacy/exploitation, digital risks, decision errors), with liability puzzles intensified by algorithmic opacity. Existing standards like ISO 12100:2010 are inadequate for autonomous construction machinery.
summary.gaps: There is no applied knowledge base on AI risks specific to construction, and existing AI standards, certifications, and safety bodies do not address sector-specific construction risks; international standards like ISO 12100 lack provisions for autonomous and continuously learning systems.
summary.future: Future work should design country-specific policy frameworks that account for risk perception differences and stakeholder risk tolerance, examining how identified risks interact with national regulatory environments. Research should also explore how to assign responsibility in the 'unknown space' created by opaque AI systems without over-regulating and hindering innovation.

summary.title: Challenges of upgrading craft workforce into Construction 4.0: Framework and agreements
summary.topic: Worker monitoring; Contract management
summary.ai_model: Blockchain; Deep learning; Classical ML; Other
summary.abstract: Craft workforce is the main productive factor in traditional construction. Construction 4.0 visions are based on automation and digitalisation, meaning that human site activities will require/stipulate changes. The extent to which manual tasks done by humans in construction will be replaced is uncertain. This might vary considering the context or type of work. Construction 4.0 includes craft workforce activities, as these can benefit from technology, fostering digital transformation in the short/medium term. The research scope is workforce-innovation-management using data from job sites. A framework is developed based on data future use involving electronic performance monitoring, building information modelling, smart contracts and artificial intelligence. A systematic scoping review is developed to identify legal/ethical issues in connection to technological aspects. The discussion and findings focus on General Data Protection Regulation compliance to apply the proposed framework. Optimised human-machine-controlled environments must be ethically managed by pre-established collective agreements and must rely on each worker's awareness and consent. The findings suggest that the…
summary.results: The paper concludes that implementing Construction 4.0 workforce monitoring requires ethically managed human-machine environments based on pre-established collective agreements, worker awareness, and informed consent. GDPR can act as a bottleneck to digital transformation if human/ethical aspects are improperly addressed, but can also serve as a policy tool for controlling methodologies. Trust (both system-based and cognition-based) between employers and employees is identified as a key enabler, requiring transparent objectives and clear consent protocols.
summary.gaps: The paper identifies gaps in judge-made law interpreting GDPR for workplace monitoring, ambiguity in defining 'biometric data' and 'legitimate interest' for performance monitoring, and the lack of worker-centered ethical frameworks for AI-driven construction management.
summary.future: The authors plan to validate the framework with expert feedback from diverse stakeholders and conduct real EPM field tests to gather insights from craftworkers. These inputs would help refine ethical compliant implementation strategies balancing people, processes, and technology.

summary.title: Domain-specific hierarchical text classification for supporting automated environmental compliance checking
summary.topic: BIM compliance checking; Permitting
summary.abstract: Automated environmental compliance checking requires automated extraction of rules from environmental regulatory textual documents such as energy conservation codes and EPA regulations. Automated rule extraction requires complex text processing and analysis for information extraction and subsequent formalization of the extracted information into computer-processable rules. In the proposed automated compliance checking (ACC) approach, the text is first classified into predefined categories before information extraction (IE). The advantages are that irrelevant text will be filtered out during text classification (TC) and text with similar semantic meaning will be grouped, thereby improving the efficiency and accuracy of further IE and compliance reasoning (CR). The categories used for TC are predefined in a semantic TC topic hierarchy, and the classified text is subsequently used in semantic IE and semantic CR. This paper presents the proposed machine learning (ML)-based TC algorithm for classifying clauses in environmental regulatory documents based on the TC topic hierarchy. In developing the algorithm, different text preprocessing techniques, ML algorithms, and performance…
summary.results: The final classifier achieved approximately 97% average recall and 84% average precision on testing data when classifying clauses into 10 leaf-level energy efficiency subtopics. SVM with linear kernel combined with BOW model and TFIDF weighting outperformed other tested configurations, and both feature selection (CHI-based K-best) and domain-specific stopword removal were effective performance improvement strategies. The bigram model underperformed compared to BOW, and modified supervised term weighting schemes did not surpass TFIDF for this application.
summary.gaps: Existing construction-domain hierarchical TC work suffers from performance drops at deeper hierarchy levels, handles only binary-transformed multilabel problems with potential data imbalance, lacks domain adaptation (e.g., domain-specific stopwords), and has not tested ensemble ML algorithms or newer supervised term weighting schemes. There is also a lack of benchmark data sets in the construction domain for comparative evaluation.
summary.future: Future work includes adapting the TC algorithm to other regulatory documents (e.g., OSHA safety standards), exploring reusability and automated construction of domain-specific stopword lists, investigating other domain adaptation approaches like feature augmentation, and developing an ontology-based TC algorithm to leverage semantic information and compare with the ML-based approach.
